steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise breakdown of the key differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar Backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose, which lacks one oxygen atom on the 2′ carbon.  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose, which has a hydroxyl (–OH) group on the 2′ carbon.  

2. Nitrogenous Bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and uracil (U) in place of thymine.  

3. Strand Structure  
   • DNA is usually double-stranded, forming a stable double helix.  
   • RNA is typically single-stranded and can fold into complex shapes (hairpins, loops).  

4. Function  
   • DNA’s main role is long-term storage and transmission of genetic information.  
   • RNA’s roles include:  
     – messenger RNA (mRNA): conveys DNA’s genetic code to ribosomes  
     – transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA): key players in protein synthesis  
     – various regulatory and catalytic RNAs (e.g., microRNA, ribozymes)  

5. Stability  
   • DNA is more chemically stable (deoxy-sugar plus double helix), which is ideal for archival storage.  
   • RNA is more prone to hydrolysis (due to the 2′-OH) and generally shorter-lived—suitable for dynamic cellular tasks.  

6. Location in Cells  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA resides primarily in the nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus (in eukaryotes) but functions throughout the cytoplasm; in prokaryotes, both DNA and RNA are in the cytoplasm.  

Summary  
DNA is the stable, double-stranded “blueprint” molecule using deoxyribose and thymine. RNA is the more versatile, generally single-stranded “worker” molecule using ribose and uracil, carrying out and regulating the steps from gene to protein.
